Reported Speech.explanation: 'How much' introduces an indirect question about price. No question word order is used.

Reported Speech.firstSentence: Everyone apart from John thought that Lisa would get the job.
Reported Speech.secondSentence: John was _____ not expect Lisa to get the job.
Reported Speech.hint: 'The only person to + verb' singles out someone who acted differently.
Reported Speech.explanation: 'The only person to' introduces the exception in a group.

Reported Speech.firstSentence: I'm concerned about whether I'll be able to finish the project on time.
Reported Speech.secondSentence: What _____ whether I'll be able to finish the project on time.
Reported Speech.hint: 'What concerns me most isâ€¦' means 'the thing that worries me most isâ€¦'
Reported Speech.explanation: 'Concern' as a verb means 'to worry or affect.' The clause subject can be 'What concerns meâ€¦'

Reported Speech.firstSentence: Last Saturday my friend asked me, 'Do you want to see a film tonight?'
Reported Speech.secondSentence: Last Saturday my friend asked me _____ a film that night.
Reported Speech.hint: Use 'whether' in reported yes/no questions.
Reported Speech.explanation: When reporting questions, change tense ('want' â†’ 'wanted') and add 'whether' or 'if' for yes/no questions.

Reported Speech.firstSentence: 'Can you help me move this sofa?' he said to me.
Reported Speech.secondSentence: He _____ help him move the sofa.
Reported Speech.hint: 'Ask someone to + verb' for reported requests.
Reported Speech.explanation: After 'ask,' use an object and infinitive when reporting a request or command.

Reported Speech.firstSentence: I asked her if she needed more information.
Reported Speech.secondSentence: I asked her if _____ she needed to know.
Reported Speech.hint: 'If there was anything elseâ€¦' is a polite indirect question form.
Reported Speech.explanation: Reported questions use normal sentence order, not question word order.

Reported Speech.firstSentence: The teacher said he was sorry he was late for the lesson.
Reported Speech.secondSentence: The teacher _____ for the lesson.
Reported Speech.hint: 'Apologise for + -ing' expresses regret for an action.
Reported Speech.explanation: After 'apologise for,' use a gerund to describe the cause of apology.

Reported Speech.firstSentence: 'Did you eat the chocolates?' Maria said to Peter.
Reported Speech.secondSentence: Maria _____ eaten the chocolates.
Reported Speech.hint: Use 'asked + person + if + clause' for yes/no questions in reported speech.
Reported Speech.explanation: In reported questions, tense and pronouns shift back.

Reported Speech.firstSentence: 'Don't forget to call me when you arrive,' she said to me.
Reported Speech.secondSentence: She _____ her when I arrived.
Reported Speech.hint: 'Tell someone to + verb' reports a command.
Reported Speech.explanation: 'Tell' takes an object and infinitive when reporting direct speech.

Reported Speech.firstSentence: 'I'll call you tomorrow,' she promised.
Reported Speech.secondSentence: She _____ the next day.
Reported Speech.hint: 'Promise to + infinitive' for reported promises.
Reported Speech.explanation: 'Promise to' is followed by an infinitive when reporting someone's commitment to do something.

Reported Speech.firstSentence: 'Don't touch that button!' he warned me.
Reported Speech.secondSentence: He _____ that button.
Reported Speech.hint: 'Warn someone not to + verb' for negative warnings.
Reported Speech.explanation: 'Warn + object + not to + infinitive' reports warnings about dangerous actions.

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: I paid far more money for my new computer than I expected to.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: I didn't expect _____ money for my new computer.
Verb Patterns.hint: After 'expect,' use 'object + to + verb' to show what was anticipated.
Verb Patterns.explanation: 'Expect' often takes 'it to + verb' when referring to an outcome or event, e.g. I didn't expect it to rain.

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: The singer dislikes people asking for his autograph in the street.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: The singer _____ people ask him for his autograph in the street.
Verb Patterns.hint: Use 'like/dislike + gerund' to talk about general preferences.
Verb Patterns.explanation: 'Like' and 'dislike' are followed by a gerund (-ing) verb form. Here, having people ask means 'when people ask.'

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: Graham likes to spend time alone just before a race.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: Graham likes to spend time _____ just before a race.
Verb Patterns.hint: Use 'by + gerund' to describe how something is done, or 'by + reflexive pronoun' to show independence.
Verb Patterns.explanation: 'By' introduces the method or state of being. 'By being alone' expresses how Graham likes to spend time; 'by himself' emphasizes doing something without others.

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: How many portraits did Picasso paint?
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: How many portraits _____ Picasso?
Verb Patterns.hint: Passive question: 'How many + were + past participle + by + subject.'
Verb Patterns.explanation: The question keeps auxiliary 'were,' adds past participle 'painted,' and uses 'by' to introduce the agent.

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: I'd rather not go out this afternoon.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: I _____ out this afternoon.
Verb Patterns.hint: Use 'feel like + -ing' for expressing what you want or don't want to do.
Verb Patterns.explanation: 'Feel like + -ing' describes preferences or mood. Negation 'don't feel like' shows unwillingness or lack of interest.

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: I promised that I would think carefully about the job offer.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: I promised _____ the job offer.
Verb Patterns.hint: 'Give thought to' means 'consider carefully.'
Verb Patterns.explanation: 'Give + noun + to' can mean 'spend time thinking about' (e.g., 'give attention to,' 'give thought to').

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: Learning to sew seemed a waste of time to Lisa.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: Lisa couldn't _____ learning to sew.
Verb Patterns.hint: Use 'see the point of + -ing' to express whether something is worth doing.
Verb Patterns.explanation: 'See the point of' takes a gerund. It means 'understand the reason or purpose.'

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: Liam has decided not to go to football practice any more.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: Liam has decided _____ to football practice.
Verb Patterns.hint: 'Give up + -ing' means to stop doing something permanently.
Verb Patterns.explanation: 'Give up' is followed by a gerund when talking about quitting an activity.

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: I promised that I would think carefully about the job offer.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: I promised _____ the job offer.
Verb Patterns.hint: 'Give thought to' means 'consider carefully.'
Verb Patterns.explanation: 'Give + noun + to' can mean 'spend time thinking about' (e.g., 'give attention to,' 'give thought to').

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: I haven't decided what sort of job I'd like to do when I leave college.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: I haven't made _____ the sort of job I'd like to do when I leave college.
Verb Patterns.hint: 'Make up your mind about' means to decide something.
Verb Patterns.explanation: The phrasal verb 'make up one's mind' is used for making decisions. 'About' introduces the topic of the decision.

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: My mother thought it would be good for me to live abroad for some time.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: My mother thought that I would _____ abroad for some time.
Verb Patterns.hint: Use 'benefit from + -ing' for positive personal gains.
Verb Patterns.explanation: 'Benefit from' is followed by a gerund when the action is general or habitual.

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: Tom was so tired that he did not even get undressed before he lay down on his bed.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: Tom was so tired that he did not even _____ before he lay down on his bed.
Verb Patterns.hint: 'Take off' means to remove clothing.
Verb Patterns.explanation: 'Take off' is a separable phrasal verb â€” the object ('his clothes') goes between 'take' and 'off.'

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: Do you object to my opening the window?
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: Do you _____ the window?
Verb Patterns.hint: 'Mind + -ing' is used to ask permission politely.
Verb Patterns.explanation: 'Mind + -ing' takes a gerund; the possessive ('my') is common before the verb.

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: I don't think we need to listen to what he has to say.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: There's _____ what he has to say.
Verb Patterns.hint: 'No point in + -ing' means something is useless or unnecessary.
Verb Patterns.explanation: After 'no point in,' use a gerund. The phrase expresses a lack of purpose or benefit.

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: Joey would rather not go to the ballgame with us.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: Joey _____ to the ballgame with us.
Verb Patterns.hint: 'Feel like + -ing' means 'want to.'
Verb Patterns.explanation: The verb 'feel like' must be followed by a gerund to show desire or preference.

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: He usually sleeps until noon.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: He _____ until noon.
Verb Patterns.hint: 'Be used to + -ing' means something is familiar or normal.
Verb Patterns.explanation: 'Be used to' is followed by a gerund when describing habits or adaptation.

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: She didn't get many people to sign the petition.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: She didn't _____ many people to sign the petition.
Verb Patterns.hint: 'Succeed in + -ing' means to achieve something.
Verb Patterns.explanation: 'Succeed in' takes a gerund, not an infinitive.

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: You can try to open the safe with that key, but it won't work.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: There's _____ the safe with that key.
Verb Patterns.hint: 'No point in + -ing' means 'it's useless to.'
Verb Patterns.explanation: 'No point in' takes a gerund when expressing futility or lack of reason.

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: The accused refused to answer questions without his lawyer.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: The accused _____ before answering any questions.
Verb Patterns.hint: 'Insist on + -ing' means to demand something firmly.
Verb Patterns.explanation: 'Insist on' must be followed by a gerund or noun, not an infinitive.

Verb Patterns.firstSentence: I couldn't persuade her to clean the house.
Verb Patterns.secondSentence: I _____ the house.
Verb Patterns.hint: 'Make + object + base verb' means 'force someone to do something.'
Verb Patterns.explanation: After 'make,' don't use 'to.' Use the base form of the verb.

Comparisons.firstSentence: Brad speaks English better than his parents do.
Comparisons.secondSentence: Brad's parents don't _____ he does.
Comparisons.hint: Think of comparing ability or skill using 'asâ€¦as.'
Comparisons.explanation: To compare actions or abilities, use 'as + adverb + as.' The negative form shows that someone is not as good as another.

Comparisons.firstSentence: Lily is so good at swimming that she is going to train for the Olympics.
Comparisons.secondSentence: Lily _____ that she is going to train for the Olympics.
Comparisons.hint: Compare 'so + adjective' with 'such + adjective + noun.'
Comparisons.explanation: 'Such + adjective + noun + that' emphasizes quality or degree. It replaces 'so + adjective + that' when a noun follows.

Comparisons.firstSentence: Sandra's sister can ski better than she can.
Comparisons.secondSentence: Sandra is _____ as her sister.
Comparisons.hint: Use 'not such a(n) + noun' for comparisons involving qualities or abilities.
Comparisons.explanation: 'Such a + noun' intensifies a description. When comparing negatively, use 'not such a(n)' to show a lower degree of ability or quality.

Comparisons.firstSentence: No matter how hard he tried, Victor couldn't open the box.
Comparisons.secondSentence: Even _____, Victor couldn't open the box.
Comparisons.hint: 'Even + very best' is used for strong emphasis in comparisons.
Comparisons.explanation: 'His very best' intensifies the noun 'efforts.' It means that even when trying as hard as possible, the outcome didn't change.

Comparisons.firstSentence: The phone was cheaper than I expected.
Comparisons.secondSentence: The phone was _____ I expected.
Comparisons.hint: Use 'not as + adjective + as' for comparisons showing difference.
Comparisons.explanation: The structure 'not asâ€¦as' means something is of a lower degree than expected.

Comparisons.firstSentence: My brother doesn't play tennis now as well as he used to.
Comparisons.secondSentence: My brother used to _____ does now.
Comparisons.hint: Use 'play better than' for comparisons of skill or ability.
Comparisons.explanation: Comparatives use '-er than' or 'more + adjective + than.' Here, 'play better than he does now' compares past and present ability.

Comparisons.firstSentence: That was one of the best meals I've had this year.
Comparisons.secondSentence: I've had very _____ that one this year.
Comparisons.hint: 'As + adjective + as' shows equality in comparison.
Comparisons.explanation: 'As good as' compares similarity in quality; 'few' emphasizes rarity of equal experiences.

Comparisons.firstSentence: The journey was shorter than I had expected.
Comparisons.secondSentence: The journey was _____ I had expected.
Comparisons.hint: Use 'not as + adjective + as' to express a weaker degree of comparison.
Comparisons.explanation: 'Not as long as' contrasts two things by showing one is less in degree.

Comparisons.firstSentence: I had expected to enjoy the film more than I did.
Comparisons.secondSentence: The film was _____ I had expected.
Comparisons.hint: 'Not as + adjective + as' shows a smaller degree.
Comparisons.explanation: It's a standard structure for negative comparisons in English.

Comparisons.firstSentence: Sarah is taller than Jane.
Comparisons.secondSentence: Jane is not _____ Sarah.
Comparisons.hint: 'Not as + adjective + as' means 'less than.'
Comparisons.explanation: 'As...as' compares equality; adding 'not' makes it negative.

Comparisons.firstSentence: He was the kindest person I had ever seen.
Comparisons.secondSentence: I had _____ person before.
Comparisons.hint: 'Such a + adjective + noun' emphasizes quality.
Comparisons.explanation: 'Such a' intensifies adjectives before singular countable nouns.

Comparisons.firstSentence: The office was too small for a meeting of the whole staff.
Comparisons.secondSentence: The office _____ for a meeting of the whole staff.
Comparisons.hint: 'Not + adjective + enough' expresses insufficiency.
Comparisons.explanation: 'Enough' follows adjectives and means 'sufficient to.'

Comparisons.firstSentence: People don't play any board games today.
Comparisons.secondSentence: Board games _____ today.
Comparisons.hint: Use 'be popular' to talk about trends or social preference.
Comparisons.explanation: The adjective 'popular' describes how liked or fashionable something is.

Comparisons.firstSentence: John and his wife seem to have no similarities.
Comparisons.secondSentence: John and his wife seem _____ with each other.
Comparisons.hint: 'Have something in common' means 'share similarities.'
Comparisons.explanation: 'Have in common' is a fixed phrase used for shared traits or experiences.

Comparisons.firstSentence: My sister doesn't like computer games very much.
Comparisons.secondSentence: My sister _____ computer games.
Comparisons.hint: 'Be keen on' = 'like or enjoy.'
Comparisons.explanation: 'Keen on + noun/-ing' expresses interest or enthusiasm.

Comparisons.firstSentence: I expected this hotel to be different from the one in Madrid.
Comparisons.secondSentence: This hotel _____ the one in Madrid.
Comparisons.hint: 'Be the same as' = 'be identical to.'
Comparisons.explanation: The expression 'the same as' contrasts with 'different from.'

Comparisons.firstSentence: No other city in the country is as large as the capital.
Comparisons.secondSentence: The capital is _____ in the country.
Comparisons.hint: Use superlative 'largest' for the highest degree.
Comparisons.explanation: 'No other...as large as' = 'the largest.' Superlatives show the maximum degree in a group.

Comparisons.firstSentence: This exercise is less difficult than the previous one.
Comparisons.secondSentence: This exercise is _____ the previous one.
Comparisons.hint: 'Less difficult' = 'easier.' Use comparative form.
Comparisons.explanation: Opposites in comparison: 'less difficult' can be expressed positively as 'easier than.'

Comparisons.firstSentence: I've never seen a more beautiful sunset than this one.
Comparisons.secondSentence: This is _____ sunset I've ever seen.
Comparisons.hint: 'Never seen a more...than' = 'the most.'
Comparisons.explanation: Superlative form: 'the most + adjective' expresses the highest degree of quality.

Comparisons.firstSentence: Your brother is just as intelligent as you are.
Comparisons.secondSentence: You are not _____ intelligent than your brother.
Comparisons.hint: 'Just as...as' = 'not much more...than.'
Comparisons.explanation: 'Much' intensifies comparatives. 'Not much more' shows near equality between two things.

Tenses.firstSentence: I had no idea that a famous film star was born in the town.
Tenses.secondSentence: I _____ that a famous film star was born in the town.
Tenses.hint: Use 'be unaware (of)' as the opposite of 'know.'
Tenses.explanation: 'Be unaware of' means 'not know about.' When followed by a noun or clause, it connects smoothly to explain what information was missing.

Tenses.firstSentence: John qualified as an instructor three years ago.
Tenses.secondSentence: John _____ instructor for three years.
Tenses.hint: Use 'has/have been' to show a continuing state that started in the past.
Tenses.explanation: 'Has been' + time period expresses something that began in the past and continues to the present â€” here, John became and still is an instructor.

Tenses.firstSentence: Although we thought the minibus would be comfortable, we were mistaken.
Tenses.secondSentence: The minibus did _____ as comfortable as we had expected.
Tenses.hint: Use 'turn out to be' to describe an unexpected or surprising result.
Tenses.explanation: The phrasal verb 'turn out to be' means the final result is different from what was expected. Negating it ('did not turn out to be') shows disappointment.

Tenses.firstSentence: Faye hadn't finished her dinner when Steve called her.
Tenses.secondSentence: Faye _____ her dinner when Steve called her.
Tenses.hint: Use 'was still + -ing' to describe an unfinished action interrupted by another.
Tenses.explanation: The past continuous ('was + -ing') shows an ongoing action in the past. 'Still' emphasizes that the action wasn't finished at the time.

Tenses.firstSentence: Christina had never visited Venice before.
Tenses.secondSentence: It was _____ to Venice.
Tenses.hint: Use 'It was her first time/visit' to describe a first experience.
Tenses.explanation: The phrase 'It was her first visit/time/trip' expresses that the event hadn't happened before. The past simple 'was' matches the original context.

Tenses.firstSentence: She found the photographs when she was cleaning her room.
Tenses.secondSentence: She _____ when she was cleaning her room.
Tenses.hint: 'Come across' means to find something unexpectedly.
Tenses.explanation: 'Come across' is a phrasal verb meaning 'discover by chance.' The object pronoun (them) follows directly.

Tenses.firstSentence: Louise didn't really feel like going out for a meal.
Tenses.secondSentence: Louise wasn't really _____ going out for a meal.
Tenses.hint: Use 'in the mood for + noun/verb-ing' to express desire or willingness.
Tenses.explanation: 'Be in the mood for' describes readiness or desire for something.

Tenses.firstSentence: Louise didn't really feel like going out for a meal.
Tenses.secondSentence: Louise wasn't really _____ going out for a meal.
Tenses.hint: Use 'in the mood for + noun/verb-ing' to express desire or willingness.
Tenses.explanation: 'Be in the mood for' describes readiness or desire for something.

Tenses.firstSentence: Louise didn't really feel like going out for a meal.
Tenses.secondSentence: Louise wasn't really _____ going out for a meal.
Tenses.hint: Use 'in the mood for + noun/verb-ing' to express desire or willingness.
Tenses.explanation: 'Be in the mood for' describes readiness or desire for something.

Tenses.firstSentence: The number of students going to university went up last year.
Tenses.secondSentence: There _____ the number of students going to university last year.
Tenses.hint: 'An increase in' changes the verb 'went up' to a noun form.
Tenses.explanation: When turning verbs into nouns, use 'an increase in + noun' for rising numbers.

Tenses.firstSentence: 'There's been a rise of over ten per cent in the price of the tickets,' said Sue.
Tenses.secondSentence: Sue said that the price of the tickets _____ than ten per cent this year.
Tenses.hint: 'Go up' means 'increase.' Use past perfect after reporting verbs.
Tenses.explanation: In reported speech, present perfect ('has gone up') changes to past perfect ('had gone up').

Tenses.firstSentence: He moved to Paris two years ago.
Tenses.secondSentence: He _____ in Paris for two years.
Tenses.hint: 'Have/has + past participle' shows an action continuing up to now.
Tenses.explanation: Use present perfect for an action that began in the past and continues to the present.

Tenses.firstSentence: I had not expected to find learning English so interesting.
Tenses.secondSentence: I am more _____ I had expected.
Tenses.hint: Use 'interested in + -ing' to express engagement in an activity.
Tenses.explanation: 'Interested in' is followed by a gerund to show the activity that causes interest. The comparison 'than I had expected' contrasts degrees.

Tenses.firstSentence: Computers are much cheaper than they were a few years ago.
Tenses.secondSentence: Computers _____ a few years ago.
Tenses.hint: 'Used to + verb' describes a past state that has changed.
Tenses.explanation: Use 'used to + base verb' for habits or situations no longer true.

Tenses.firstSentence: Getting in shape will take longer than you think.
Tenses.secondSentence: You won't be able to _____ as you think.
Tenses.hint: Use 'as...as' to show equal or unequal speed or degree.
Tenses.explanation: Comparative 'as fast as' contrasts two time frames.

Tenses.firstSentence: She wasn't the least bit surprised to find out that her husband had an affair.
Tenses.secondSentence: It wasn't _____ to find out that her husband had an affair.
Tenses.hint: Use 'It was a surprise forâ€¦' to express reaction or emotion.
Tenses.explanation: 'It was a surprise for someone to + verb' expresses emotional response to an event.

Tenses.firstSentence: When I studied at university, I never had enough money.
Tenses.secondSentence: When I studied at university, I _____.
Tenses.hint: 'Be short of' = 'not have enough of something.'
Tenses.explanation: 'Be short of' is a set phrase expressing scarcity.

Tenses.firstSentence: What's the answer to sixteen minus eight?
Tenses.secondSentence: If you _____ sixteen, what's the answer?
Tenses.hint: 'Take away from' means to subtract.
Tenses.explanation: The phrasal verb 'take away' functions as 'subtract' in mathematics.

Tenses.firstSentence: The students will finish their English course at the end of June.
Tenses.secondSentence: The English course _____ the beginning of July.
Tenses.hint: 'Will have + past participle' is used for future perfect tense.
Tenses.explanation: Future perfect expresses an action completed before a future time.

Tenses.firstSentence: Bob hadn't seen his uncle for several years.
Tenses.secondSentence: After several years _____ , Bob saw his uncle again.
Tenses.hint: 'After several years had gone by' = 'after several years passed.'
Tenses.explanation: The past perfect 'had gone by' marks a time that finished before another past event.

Tenses.firstSentence: It's now a year since he started learning English.
Tenses.secondSentence: He _____ English for a year now.
Tenses.hint: 'Has been + -ing' shows duration from past to present.
Tenses.explanation: The present perfect continuous links a past start point to now, emphasizing duration.

Linking Words.firstSentence: Simon was the only student to apply for a scholarship.
Linking Words.secondSentence: Apart _____ the students applied for a scholarship.
Linking Words.hint: Use 'apart from' and 'none of' to show exclusion.
Linking Words.explanation: 'Apart from + noun' introduces the exception, and 'none of + plural noun' confirms zero quantity. Together, they show Simon was the only one.

Linking Words.firstSentence: Debbie wore a jumper because she thought it might be cold in the mountains.
Linking Words.secondSentence: Debbie wore a jumper _____ it was cold in the mountains.
Linking Words.hint: Use 'in case' to express precaution â€” doing something because something might happen.
Linking Words.explanation: 'In case + clause' introduces a reason for doing something as a precaution. It's not the same as 'if,' which expresses condition, not preparation.

Linking Words.firstSentence: Grace knows a lot about Web design, even though she has never studied it.
Linking Words.secondSentence: Despite _____ , Grace knows a lot about Web design.
Linking Words.hint: After 'despite,' use a gerund (-ing) or 'having + past participle' for contrast.
Linking Words.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun or gerund phrase. 'Having studied' (or 'never having studied') compresses 'even though she has never studied.'

Linking Words.firstSentence: The tour bus stopped frequently to let people admire the view.
Linking Words.secondSentence: The tour bus stopped frequently _____ admire the view.
Linking Words.hint: Use 'so that + subject + could' to show purpose.
Linking Words.explanation: 'So that' introduces the reason for an action, followed by a clause with 'could' when referring to ability or purpose.

Linking Words.firstSentence: The ferry couldn't sail because the weather was bad.
Linking Words.secondSentence: The ferry couldn't sail _____ weather.
Linking Words.hint: Use 'due to + noun phrase' to explain a reason.
Linking Words.explanation: 'Due to' functions as a preposition meaning 'because of.' It must be followed by a noun, not a clause.

Linking Words.firstSentence: Ashley always eats a big breakfast before going out in the morning.
Linking Words.secondSentence: Ashley never goes out in the morning _____ a big breakfast.
Linking Words.hint: Use 'without + -ing' to describe what doesn't happen before another action.
Linking Words.explanation: 'Without + -ing' introduces a negative condition or circumstance.

Linking Words.firstSentence: Ashley always eats a big breakfast before going out in the morning.
Linking Words.secondSentence: Ashley never goes out in the morning _____ a big breakfast.
Linking Words.hint: Use 'without + -ing' to describe what doesn't happen before another action.
Linking Words.explanation: 'Without + -ing' introduces a negative condition or circumstance.

Linking Words.firstSentence: The group continued to walk despite rain starting to fall.
Linking Words.secondSentence: The group carried _____ started to rain.
Linking Words.hint: Use 'even though' to contrast two ideas ('despite the fact thatâ€¦').
Linking Words.explanation: 'Even though' introduces a contrast, similar to 'although.'

Linking Words.firstSentence: Almost all the tickets for next Saturday's concert have been sold.
Linking Words.secondSentence: There are _____ for next Saturday's concert.
Linking Words.hint: 'Hardly any' means 'almost none.'
Linking Words.explanation: 'Hardly any' + plural noun expresses a very small quantity.

Linking Words.firstSentence: He sings in the show and dances in it as well.
Linking Words.secondSentence: Not _____ in the show, he also dances in it.
Linking Words.hint: 'Not only... but also' emphasizes multiple actions.
Linking Words.explanation: Inversion ('does he sing') follows 'not only' for emphasis in formal writing or speech.

Linking Words.firstSentence: I was late for work because I missed my bus.
Linking Words.secondSentence: I was late for work _____ my bus.
Linking Words.hint: 'On account of' means 'because of.'
Linking Words.explanation: 'On account of' is followed by a gerund when explaining a reason.

Linking Words.firstSentence: The letter has nothing to do with you.
Linking Words.secondSentence: The letter is _____ to you.
Linking Words.hint: 'Of no concern' means 'irrelevant' or 'not your business.'
Linking Words.explanation: 'Be of + noun' is a formal structure meaning 'have the quality of.'

Linking Words.firstSentence: Everyone came to the party apart from Cathy.
Linking Words.secondSentence: Everyone came to the party _____ Cathy.
Linking Words.hint: 'With the exception of' means 'except for.'
Linking Words.explanation: The phrase introduces an excluded person or thing from a group.

Linking Words.firstSentence: Honestly, I don't mind where we go for our summer holidays.
Linking Words.secondSentence: Honestly, _____ me where we go for our summer holidays.
Linking Words.hint: 'It doesn't matter to me' = 'I don't mind.'
Linking Words.explanation: 'Matter' acts as a verb meaning 'to be important to someone.'

Linking Words.firstSentence: We came early so that we could get good seats.
Linking Words.secondSentence: We came early _____ get good seats.
Linking Words.hint: 'In order to' = 'so that we could.'
Linking Words.explanation: 'In order to + infinitive' expresses purpose formally.

Linking Words.firstSentence: Although it was expensive, I bought the jacket.
Linking Words.secondSentence: I bought the jacket _____ expensive.
Linking Words.hint: 'In spite of' + noun/gerund shows contrast.
Linking Words.explanation: 'In spite of' is followed by a noun or gerund phrase, not a clause. It means 'although.'

Linking Words.firstSentence: Because of the traffic, we arrived late.
Linking Words.secondSentence: The traffic was heavy, and _____ we arrived late.
Linking Words.hint: 'As a result' shows consequence or effect.
Linking Words.explanation: 'As a result' connects a cause to its consequence, similar to 'therefore' or 'consequently.'

Linking Words.firstSentence: She studied hard, so she passed the exam.
Linking Words.secondSentence: She studied hard and _____ the exam.
Linking Words.hint: 'Therefore' shows logical result or conclusion.
Linking Words.explanation: 'Therefore' is a formal linking word meaning 'for that reason' or 'as a result.'

Linking Words.firstSentence: Besides being expensive, the hotel was poorly located.
Linking Words.secondSentence: The hotel was expensive and, _____, poorly located.
Linking Words.hint: 'In addition' adds extra information.
Linking Words.explanation: 'In addition' introduces additional points, similar to 'also' or 'furthermore.'

Linking Words.firstSentence: While I understand your concerns, I disagree with your solution.
Linking Words.secondSentence: _____ I understand your concerns, I disagree with your solution.
Linking Words.hint: 'Even though' emphasizes contrast more than 'while.'
Linking Words.explanation: 'Even though' introduces a concession, showing contrast between two ideas.

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: Ursula was disappointed not to win the competition.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: Not winning the competition _____ to Ursula.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: Think of idiomatic expressions like 'come as a surprise/disappointment.'
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: The phrase 'come as + noun' expresses emotional reactions â€” e.g. come as a surprise / came as a disappointment.

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: It's very hard for Alex to get up in the morning.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: Alex _____ up in the morning.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: Use 'have trouble + -ing' to express difficulty doing something.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: The phrase 'have trouble' is followed by a gerund (-ing) verb. It shows ongoing difficulty or effort needed to complete an action.

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: I went to the dentist's because I couldn't stand the toothache any longer.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: I couldn't _____ the toothache any longer, so I went to the dentist's.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: Think of a phrasal verb meaning 'tolerate.'
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: 'Put up with' means to tolerate or endure something unpleasant. The three-word phrasal verb must stay together for correct meaning.

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: Heidi stayed with a friend when she went to London.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: A friend _____ when she went to London.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: Think of the phrasal verb meaning 'give someone accommodation.'
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: 'Put someone up' is a phrasal verb meaning to let someone stay at your house. The pronoun 'her' must come between 'put' and 'up.'

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: Is it all right if I turn the television off?
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: Would _____ the television off?
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: Use 'Would you mind + -ing' or 'Would you mind if + past tense' for polite requests.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: 'Would you mind' forms polite questions. It's followed by either a gerund or 'if + past tense' clause. Both express courtesy when asking permission.

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: Damon looked so funny in his brother's tracksuit that we had to laugh.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: We _____ at Damon because he looked so funny in his brother's tracksuit.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: 'Can't / couldn't help + -ing' means you can't stop yourself from doing something.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: 'Can't help + -ing' shows an uncontrollable reaction or emotion. The preposition 'at' completes the idea when directed toward someone.

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: Dancing was an activity that David had never wanted to do.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: Dancing was an activity that _____ David.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: 'Appeal to' means to attract or interest someone.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: The phrasal verb 'appeal to' means to be interesting or pleasing. The preposition 'to' must follow; omitting it makes the structure incorrect.

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: You are welcome to contact me if you need more information.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: Please feel free _____ me if you need more information.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: 'Get in touch with' means to contact or communicate.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: 'Get in touch with + person' expresses contacting someone informally. The infinitive form 'to get' follows 'feel free.'

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: During the quiz, I could not think of the correct answer to the winning question.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: During the quiz, I was not _____ the correct answer to the winning question.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: 'Come up with' means to think of an idea or solution.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: 'Be able to + verb' expresses ability. The phrasal verb 'come up with' means 'think of.'

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: Tony never took any notice of the advice people gave him.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: Tony never _____ the advice people gave him.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: 'Pay attention to' means to notice or focus on something.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: 'Pay attention to' is a fixed collocation meaning 'listen or consider carefully.'

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: 'Last week, I unexpectedly met an old friend on the train,' said the man.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: The man said that _____ an old friend on the train unexpectedly last week.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: 'Run into' means 'meet someone by chance.'
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: 'Run into' is a phrasal verb for unexpected encounters.

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: I'll phone you tonight so you can tell me what you've been doing.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: I'll phone you tonight to _____ news.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: 'Catch up on' means to hear about or get updated on something.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: The phrasal verb 'catch up on' is used with nouns like 'work' or 'news.'

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: I am sorry I didn't contact you, but I was very busy.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: I apologise for _____ you, but I was very busy.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: 'Get in touch with' means to contact someone.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: The negative form 'not getting in touch with' acts as a gerund phrase after 'apologise for.'

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: Helen finally managed to think of a solution to her problem.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: Helen finally succeeded _____ a solution to her problem.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: 'Come up with' means to invent or think of an idea.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: 'Succeed in + -ing' describes successful effort. 'Come up with' completes the idea.

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: Please complete this form.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: Please _____ this form.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: 'Fill up' or 'fill in' means to complete information on a document.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: 'Fill in' and 'fill up' are phrasal verbs commonly used with 'form' or 'application.'

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: Famous people are always recognised no matter where they go.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: Famous people _____ no matter where they go.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: 'Can't avoid + -ing' expresses inevitability.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: After 'avoid,' use a gerund; 'can't avoid' means 'impossible to prevent.'

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: He doesn't appreciate anything.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: He takes _____.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: 'Take for granted' = 'not value something properly.'
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: The idiom means assuming something will always exist or stay the same.

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: We must take as much advantage as possible of any opportunity to speak English.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: We have _____ any opportunity to speak English.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: Use 'make the most of' to mean 'use fully.'
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: 'Make the most of' means to use time or opportunity in the best possible way.

Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.firstSentence: Don't stop trying to improve your English.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.secondSentence: Don't _____ to improve your English.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.hint: 'Give up + -ing' means to stop doing something.
Phrasal Verbs \u0026 Expressions.explanation: 'Give up' is followed by a gerund when describing abandoned activities.
